learn: The two phases of generation: prefill and decode
Why decoding is limited by memory bandwidth
Shrinking the cache with MQA, GQA and MLA
intro.why: Serving a model means turning a probability distribution into text, quickly and cheaply. The decoding rule shapes output quality; the KV cache and memory bandwidth decide speed, cost and how many users fit on a GPU.

sections.title: Prefill and decode phases
sections.plain: First the model reads the whole prompt at once; then it writes the answer one token at a time.
sections.body:
Autoregressive generation has two phases:

  • Prefill: the whole prompt is processed in one parallel forward pass. Large matrix multiplications keep the GPU busy (compute-bound). Keys and values for every prompt token are stored in the KV cache. Its duration drives the time to first token (TTFT).
  • Decode: one new token per step. Only the newest token is pushed through the network; it attends to all cached keys and values, and its own K/V are appended. Each step reads all weights for a small amount of arithmetic (bandwidth-bound). Its speed is the time per output token (TPOT).

Without the KV cache, every step would recompute keys and values for the entire prefix, so generating n tokens would cost O(n²) forward work instead of O(n). Generation stops at an end-of-sequence token or a length limit.

sections.title: Greedy and beam search
sections.plain: Greedy always takes the single most likely next word; beam search keeps a few candidate sentences in play.
sections.body:
Greedy decoding picks argmax at each step: fast and deterministic, but it can commit early to a path whose continuation is poor. Beam search keeps the B highest-probability partial sequences, expands each, and keeps the best B again, approximating the most likely whole sequence.

Worked: step 1 offers A (0.6) or B (0.4). After A the options are flat (0.3, 0.3, 0.4); after B, x has 0.9. Greedy takes A then z: 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24. Beam width 2 keeps B and finds B x = 0.4 × 0.9 = 0.36.

Beam search suits tasks with one right output (translation, summarisation with tight references). For open-ended text, maximising likelihood produces bland, repetitive output, so sampling is preferred. Long beams also favour short outputs unless a length penalty is applied.

sections.title: Top-k sampling
sections.plain: Sample only from the k most likely words.
sections.body:
Sampling draws the next token from the model's distribution, giving variety. Pure sampling occasionally picks very unlikely tokens from the long tail, which derails text. Top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens, renormalises their probabilities and samples among them.

With (0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10) and k = 2: keep 0.5 and 0.25 → 0.667 and 0.333. k = 1 is greedy. The weakness is that k is fixed: when the model is confident (one token at 0.95) k = 40 still admits junk; when it is uncertain (many plausible words) a small k cuts good options.

sections.title: Top-p (nucleus) sampling
sections.plain: Keep the smallest group of likely words whose probabilities add up to p.
sections.body:
Top-p (nucleus) sampling sorts tokens by probability and keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p, then renormalises and samples. The set size adapts: few tokens when the model is confident, many when it is unsure.

Worked: p = 0.9 on (0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10). Cumulative 0.5, 0.75, 0.90 → keep 3 tokens, drop the last. Renormalised: 0.5/0.9 = 0.556, 0.278, 0.167.

Typical chat settings combine temperature ≈ 0.7–1.0 with p ≈ 0.9–0.95. Related variants include min-p (keep tokens above a fraction of the top probability).

sections.title: Temperature
sections.plain: Temperature makes the model's choices sharper (low) or more adventurous (high).
sections.body:
Temperature divides logits before the softmax:

$$P(i) = \frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}}$$

T < 1 sharpens the distribution (more predictable), T > 1 flattens it (more diverse, more errors), and T → 0 approaches greedy. On (0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10): T = 0.5 gives a top probability of 0.725; T = 2 gives 0.37.

Use low temperature for code, extraction, maths and evaluation; moderate temperature with top-p for conversation and creative writing. Temperature reshapes; top-k/top-p truncate. They are usually applied in that order.

sections.title: The memory-bandwidth bottleneck
sections.plain: Each new word requires reading all the model's weights from memory, and that reading, not the maths, is the slow part.
sections.body:
During decode, each step multiplies one token's vector by every weight matrix: about 2 FLOPs per parameter but one full read of every weight. The arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte read) at batch 1 in 16-bit is about 1, while GPUs need roughly 100+ to be compute-bound. So the GPU waits on memory.

Worked: a 7B model in 16-bit has 14 GB of weights. At 2 TB/s bandwidth one pass takes 7 ms, so one sequence cannot exceed ~143 tokens/s, however many FLOPs the GPU offers.

Consequences: batching shares one weight read across many sequences (raising intensity and throughput); quantization shrinks the bytes to read; the KV cache adds more bytes per step as contexts grow. Prefill, by contrast, processes many tokens per weight read and is compute-bound.

sections.title: KV-cache size
sections.plain: The cache stores a key and value for every token in every layer, and it gets big fast.
sections.body:
Per token the cache stores one key and one value vector in every layer:

$$\text{KV bytes/token} = 2 \times L \times (n_{kv}\, d_{head}) \times \text{bytes}$$

Worked: 32 layers, width 4096, 16-bit: 2 × 32 × 4096 × 2 = 524,288 bytes ≈ 0.5 MiB per token. 2048 tokens ≈ 1 GiB per sequence; 32k tokens ≈ 16 GiB; 16 users at 8k tokens ≈ 64 GiB, more than a 7B model's weights.

The cache grows linearly with context length and with the number of concurrent sequences, and it is read in full every decode step. It is therefore often the limit on batch size and context in serving, which motivates paged allocation (M6), cache quantization and the head-sharing schemes below.

sections.title: MQA, GQA and MLA
sections.plain: Let many query heads share fewer key/value heads, or store a compressed summary, so the cache is smaller.
sections.body:
Standard multi-head attention (MHA) gives each of H query heads its own key and value heads. Variants shrink the cache:

  • Multi-query attention (MQA): all query heads share one K/V head: cache H× smaller (32× with 32 heads), some quality loss.
  • Grouped-query attention (GQA): G groups of query heads share G K/V heads (e.g. 8 groups → 4× smaller); near-MHA quality, the common compromise.
  • Multi-head latent attention (MLA): store a low-dimensional latent per token (e.g. 512 numbers per layer) and project it up to keys and values when needed: a large cut (≈16× here) while keeping per-head diversity.

Smaller caches mean more concurrent users, longer contexts and faster decode (fewer bytes to read).

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Repetition penalties and frequency/presence penalties discourage loops in sampled text.
  • Seeds and determinism: even greedy decoding can differ across hardware or batch composition due to floating-point order.
  • Sliding-window caches keep only recent tokens' K/V for windowed layers.
  • Temperature 0 is not "more correct"; it is just more deterministic, and can loop.

code.title: Greedy, beam, top-k, top-p and temperature
code.explain: Applies top-p 0.9 to (0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10) (keeps 3, renormalised 0.556/0.278/0.167), top-k 2, temperatures 0.5/1/2 (top probability 0.725/0.5/0.37), shows beam width 2 finding B x (0.36) where greedy settles for A z (0.24), and draws samples.
code.notes: Toy distributions, not a real model.
code.code:
"""Decoding strategies on a toy next-token distribution: greedy, beam search, top-k, top-p and temperature."""
import numpy as np

def softmax(z, T=1.0):
    z = np.asarray(z, float) / T
    e = np.exp(z - z.max())
    return e / e.sum()

# Top-p (nucleus) on a sorted distribution
vocab = ["cat", "dog", "fox", "owl"]
p = np.array([0.50, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10])
def top_p(p, thr):
    idx = np.argsort(-p); c = np.cumsum(p[idx])
    k = int(np.searchsorted(c, thr - 1e-12) + 1)
    keep = idx[:k]; q = np.zeros_like(p); q[keep] = p[keep] / p[keep].sum()
    return keep, q
keep, q = top_p(p, 0.9)
print("top-p 0.9 keeps:", [vocab[i] for i in keep], "cumulative", round(p[keep].sum(), 2))
print("renormalised  :", ", ".join(f"{w} {v:.3f}" for w, v in zip(vocab, q)))

def top_k(p, k):
    keep = np.argsort(-p)[:k]; q = np.zeros_like(p); q[keep] = p[keep] / p[keep].sum(); return q
print("top-k 2       :", ", ".join(f"{w} {v:.3f}" for w, v in zip(vocab, top_k(p, 2))))

# Temperature reshapes the distribution
logits = np.log(p)
for T in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
    print(f"T = {T}: ", softmax(logits, T).round(3), " max prob", round(softmax(logits, T).max(), 3))

# Greedy vs beam search on a two-step toy model
step1 = {"A": 0.6, "B": 0.4}
step2 = {"A": {"x": 0.3, "y": 0.3, "z": 0.4}, "B": {"x": 0.9, "y": 0.05, "z": 0.05}}
g1 = max(step1, key=step1.get); g2 = max(step2[g1], key=step2[g1].get)
print(f"greedy: {g1} {g2}  prob {step1[g1]*step2[g1][g2]:.2f}")
beams = sorted(((a, b, step1[a]*step2[a][b]) for a in step1 for b in step2[a]), key=lambda t: -t[2])[:2]
for a, b, pr in beams: print(f"beam (width 2) candidate: {a} {b}  prob {pr:.2f}")
print("beam search finds the higher-probability sequence B x (0.36) that greedy (A z, 0.24) misses")

# Sampling variety
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
draws = rng.choice(vocab, size=20, p=q)
print("20 samples with top-p 0.9:", " ".join(draws))

code.title: KV cache, shared heads and bandwidth
code.explain: Computes 524,288 bytes per token for a 32-layer, 4096-wide model (1 GiB at 2048 tokens), the savings of GQA (4×), MQA (32×) and an MLA-style latent (16×), and the bandwidth bound: 14 GB of weights at 2 TB/s → 7 ms/token → ≤ 143 tokens/s.
mistakes: Counting only K or only V.
Ignoring batch size when sizing the cache.
code.notes: Real systems add overheads and fragmentation.
code.code:
"""KV-cache size, MQA/GQA/MLA savings, and why decoding is memory-bandwidth bound."""
# KV cache per token = 2 (K and V) x layers x hidden x bytes
L, d, b = 32, 4096, 2
per_tok = 2 * L * d * b
print(f"KV cache per token: 2 x {L} x {d} x {b} = {per_tok:,} bytes = {per_tok/2**20:.2f} MiB")
for n in (2048, 8192, 32768):
    print(f"  {n:6d} tokens -> {per_tok*n/2**30:6.2f} GiB per sequence")
print(f"  batch of 16 at 8192 tokens -> {per_tok*8192*16/2**30:.0f} GiB")

# Grouped / multi-query attention share K,V heads
H, hd = 32, 128
for name, kv in (("multi-head (MHA)", 32), ("grouped-query (GQA, 8 groups)", 8), ("multi-query (MQA)", 1)):
    t = 2 * L * kv * hd * b
    print(f"{name:30s}: {kv:2d} KV heads -> {t:,} bytes/token ({H//kv}x smaller than MHA)")
lat = 512
print(f"latent compression (MLA, latent {lat}): {L*lat*b:,} bytes/token (~{per_tok//(L*lat*b)}x smaller than MHA)")

# Decode is bandwidth bound: every token must read all weights once
params, wbytes, bw = 7e9, 2, 2.0e12
t = params * wbytes / bw
print(f"7B fp16 weights {params*wbytes/1e9:.0f} GB, bandwidth {bw/1e12:.0f} TB/s -> {t*1e3:.1f} ms/token -> <= {1/t:.0f} tokens/s for one sequence")
flops = 2 * params; ai = flops / (params * wbytes)
print(f"arithmetic intensity at batch 1: {ai:.0f} FLOP/byte (GPUs need ~100+ to be compute bound)")
for B in (1, 8, 64):
    print(f"  batch {B:3d}: intensity ~ {ai*B:5.0f} FLOP/byte")
print("prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel (compute bound); decode emits one token per step (bandwidth bound)")
